title: Analysis, transforms and special functions
organizing_question: What analytic representation makes the desired quantity computable without losing its domain, norm or normalization?
core_objects: holomorphic functions and positive spectral functions
overview:
This domain organizes the part of the archive concerned with representing an object so that a question about it becomes a controlled calculation. The representation may be a coefficient sequence, a contour integral, a special-function identity or a spectral measure. In every case, the first task is to state what is being represented and in which space. Bessel’s inequality sees an orthogonal projection; Parseval requires completeness. An atomic pairing uses cancellation in a particular measure. A Fourier transform needs a normalization, and a sampled FFT describes an interpolant before it describes any unknown continuous function. These distinctions provide constructive working rules, not merely objections to formulas. They show how to calculate the information retained by a representation and the error introduced by discarding the rest.

The first family develops that rule through transforms, frames and cancellation. Its four-coordinate Haar calculation accounts exactly for all energy and for the residual after discarding fine detail. A lower frame bound then converts a measurement discrepancy into a state discrepancy with an explicit constant. This is the analytical bridge to reconstruction, while the possibility of a nullspace explains why coefficient summaries can fail to identify an object. Weighted atoms and local Hardy–BMO estimates keep the same measure in the cancellation and pairing; directional image differences explain why a transform may be useful for an edge geometry without being a complete representation.

The second family puts local analytic certificates next to the global information they need. Cauchy extraction requires a holomorphic neighborhood; logarithmic derivatives record zeros or poles with multiplicity; contour counts do not distinguish two simple zeros from one double zero. Positive finite atomic measures give a particularly productive exact class. Their Herglotz functions have simple real poles, a fixed half-plane sign and one simple zero between each pair of poles. The proof uses only explicit signs and derivatives. Branch periods then demonstrate why locally closed differentials can still carry global continuation data.

The third family collects exact integration and special functions by method. Mellin moments, theta and modular reindexing, logarithmic integrals, dilogarithms, elliptic limits and finite trigonometric sums each retain their convergence and branch conditions. The elementary logarithmic moment supplies factorial weights and a rational tail bound for a zeta integral. Its role is to teach a reproducible reduction with a stopping rule, while the original member treatments retain the additional hypotheses needed for their richer constants.

The fourth family treats spectra as data of an operator with a domain and multiplicity. A diagonal model connects a counting function, a heat-trace exponent and a zeta half-plane. It separates fixed-time trace class from a singular short-time limit and shows why changing multiplicity changes dimension. Together, the four families suggest a practical order: fix the representation and its information loss, establish the analytic certificate, calculate with controlled tails, and only then interpret a spectral or geometric invariant. The progression entries identify dated source topics across 2023–2026; they do not date the reconstructed proofs or assert historical discovery priority.
open_frontier: The main frontier is a portable certificate that carries domains, measures, branches, multiplicities and uniform error bounds through changes of representation. The recovered material does not yet provide one general automated solver.

title: Differential equations and asymptotics
organizing_question: How does a stated equation produce a controlled solution, approximation or limiting law?
core_objects: finite asymptotic expansions and sectorial integrals
overview:
The differential-equation material becomes coherent when the equation, its state space and its boundary or initial data are treated as one object. A familiar profile is not yet a solution, and a formal operator is not yet a closed evolution law. The early hyperbolic-identity discussion is an instructive starting point: substituting a sech-squared wave into the stated KdV normalization forces its amplitude and speed. That same direct method extends to energy laws, diffusion stencils, local Frobenius recurrences and asymptotic remainders. The aim of this chapter is to make each conclusion executable as a sequence of explicit mathematical steps while preserving the assumptions that make those steps valid.

The first family begins with balances. On a periodic circle, the heat equation preserves the mean and decreases the squared fluctuation norm at a rate fixed by the first nonzero Fourier mode. The worked example has only two modes, so its solution and energy derivative can be calculated independently. Nonlinear members then alter the energy or the mobility: a Cahn–Hilliard flow preserves mass while dissipating an energy through a gradient of the chemical potential, whereas an L² gradient flow has a different dissipation law. Coupled diffusion and rotating waves add exchange or flux terms. Boundary conditions and regularity remain part of every calculation.

The second family separates the finite numerical map from its continuum interpretation. The periodic heat stencil has an exact mass identity, a sharp positivity range and an independent Fourier-symbol calculation. Taylor expansion supplies consistency only for sufficiently smooth solutions; stability and defect accumulation are then needed for a finite-time error bound. Distributed communication tests, anisotropy estimates, interpolation and inverse cutoffs are related by this error-budget viewpoint. They are not interchangeable certificates. In particular, the linked cutoff lab balances bias and amplified noise for its own observation model rather than providing a universal PDE solver.

The third family treats local singular equations through normalized bases. A coalescing Euler pair becomes regular after taking a divided difference, and its limiting logarithm has nontrivial unipotent monodromy. The Wronskian distinguishes an actual loss of independence from a bad basis. The recovered Picard–Fuchs examples supply more specific recurrences, while value–derivative matching and gauge conventions determine basis comparison. Extra harmonics in a Hill reduction remain visible instead of being silently renamed Mathieu.

The fourth family makes limiting statements quantitative. Its factorial Borel model has a divergent power series, a valid finite remainder estimate and an explicitly calculable exponential ambiguity. A cubic fold supplies a separate exact three-halves action difference and two-thirds transition scale. The elliptic logarithmic constant and perturbative discriminant questions belong to the same discipline of specified limits, although each uses a different proof. Reading these families in order moves from exact identities to stable approximation, then to local continuation and singular limits. The open task is to make estimates uniform when several of these operations are combined, rather than infer a global theorem from a local germ or a formal expansion.
open_frontier: Uniform multi-parameter error bounds, resonant basis normalization, nonlinear invariant-preserving schemes and global selection of asymptotic branches remain the central extensions.

title: Dynamics, mechanics and mathematical modeling
organizing_question: What state, metric and invariant make a dynamical claim precise and testable?
overview:
The dynamics material is organized around four choices that a model must make explicit: its state, its clock, its metric and its observations. The same eigenvalues can coexist with very different transient gains; the same geometric path can have different time parametrizations; the same observation can come from different hidden states. The archive’s strongest recurrent ideas are constructive ways to resolve these ambiguities. They include exact Lyapunov matrices, explicit period-two branches, conserved Hamiltonians, dimensionally complete mass balances and derived memory kernels. Each answers a particular question. Their connections become useful once the question and the retained state are stated before the calculation.

The stability family leads with an exact triangular matrix. Its eigenvalues are stable, its Euclidean norm can initially grow, and a positive matrix certifies decay in another norm. This gives a complete example of nonnormal amplification rather than a slogan about it. Continuous and discrete Gramians, common storage functions and hybrid dwell-time bounds extend the same reasoning. Switching incurs a logarithmic metric cost, so stability of the individual modes alone does not establish stability of every switching sequence. A two-line projection calculation supplies a further geometric model: the cycle contraction and the commutator norm are different functions of the same angle. The linked projection lab keeps that distinction visible.

The bifurcation family follows invariant branches and their multipliers. Exact logistic algebra proves the first fixed-point threshold, the born two-cycle and the next flip boundary. That substantial result is deliberately separated from the deeper infinite-cascade and universality questions. Return-map jets identify the cubic term left after a multiplier-minus-one map is composed with itself. Square-root cycle branches and the tanh pitchfork provide further local mechanisms with explicit conditions. None of these local facts alone identifies a global chaotic attractor or establishes a physical renormalization equivalence.

The mechanics and modeling family starts from conservation and units. Hamilton’s equations preserve a stated energy, and a simple turn gives different exponents for elapsed time and action because those quantities integrate reciprocal momentum and momentum respectively. Scalar RG coordinates preserve a fixed-point derivative under an invertible state-coordinate change with the same time variable; a time rescaling changes the rate. Population recurrences, radiation fluxes, drag, chemical yield and volume-to-mass calculations are organized by similarly explicit balance laws. Dimensional agreement narrows a model but does not supply its missing measurements or dimensionless coefficient.

The memory family finally asks whether a reduced state determines its future. Eliminating a hidden linear coordinate produces both a convolution kernel and a source from the hidden initial condition. Omitting them changes the equation. Mechanical words, substitutions and relative periodicity pose discrete versions of the retained-information question. A balanced aperiodic rotation coding can be completely deterministic and have an exact frequency, so irregular appearance is not a chaos certificate. Across these four families, the dated progression traces changing source topics from 2023 onward; the present proofs and worked models are a new organization of that material, with their scope stated independently of historical attribution.
open_frontier: The most useful next step is to combine certified basins, physically meaningful transient norms and minimal sufficient reduced states for specific models, with quantitative memory-approximation bounds.
